items.readable_text:
Content:
The greatest common factor (or [MATH: \textrm{GCF}]) of two integers is the largest positive integer that divides both of them.

Content:
For example, the greatest common factor of [MATH: 12] and [MATH: 30] is [MATH: 6.] This is because [MATH: 6] is the greatest integer that divides both [MATH: 12] and [MATH: 30.] We can write this as
[MATH: \textrm{GCF}(12,30) = 6.]

Content:
There is a general technique that we can use to find the greatest common factor of any two integers. All we need to do is find the prime factorization of both numbers and multiply the prime factors that appear in both factorizations.

Content:
For example, the prime factorizations of [MATH: 12] and [MATH: 30] are as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 12|= 2_(―) ⋅ 2 ⋅ 3_(―); 30|= 2_(―) ⋅ 3_(―) ⋅ 5]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: 12] and [MATH: 30] both have the factors of [MATH: {\color{blue}2}] and [MATH: {\color{red}3}] in common. Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{GCF}(12,30) = {\color{blue}2}\cdot {\color{red}3} = 6.]

Content:
Sometimes, we write "[MATH: \textrm{gcd}]" instead of [MATH: \textrm{GCF}.] They mean the same thing, but [MATH: \textrm{gcd}] stands for greatest common divisor.

items.title: Finding the Greatest Common Factor of Two Integers

sections.normalized_html:
To find the greatest common factor [MATH: (\textrm{GCF})] of two numbers, we first find the prime factorization of both numbers.

  • First, let's find the prime decomposition of [MATH: 420{:}]

    So, [MATH: 420=2\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7.]

  • Next, we find the prime factorization of [MATH: 84{:}]

    So, [MATH: 84=2\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot 7.]

Comparing the decompositions side-by-side, we pair off the factors as much as possible: [MATH: 420|= 2_(―) ⋅ 2_(―) ⋅ 3_(―) ⋅ 5 ⋅ 7_(―); 84|= 2_(―) ⋅ 2_(―) ⋅ 3_(―) ⋅ 7_(―)]

The common factors are [MATH: 2, 2, 3,] and [MATH: 7.] Notice that the common factor [MATH: 2] appears twice in both factorizations. Therefore,

[MATH: \textrm{GCF}(420,84) = 2\cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7 = 84.]
